'''Piro''' is a poorly attested, extinct [[Tanoan language]] once spoken in the more than twenty [[Piro Pueblos]] near [[Socorro, New Mexico]].<ref name="Harrington"/> It has generally been classified as one of the [[Tiwa languages]],<ref>Newman, Stanley (1954) "American Indian Linguistics in the Southwest" ''American Anthropologist'' New Series, 56(4): pp. 626-634, 631</ref> though Leap (1971) contested whether or not Piro is truly a Tanoan language at all.<ref>Leap, William L. (1971) "Who Were the Piro?" ''Anthropological Linguistics'' 13: pp. 321-330</ref>  The last known speaker, an elderly woman, was interviewed by Mooney in 1897, and by 1909 all Piro members had [[Mexican Spanish]] as their native language.<ref name="Harrington"/>

==Corpus==
The corpus of Piro is limited to place names, two vocabularies and an 1860 translation of the Lord's Prayer using Spanish orthography:<ref name="Harrington">{{cite journal |last1=Harrington |first1=John P. |title=Notes on the Piro Language |journal=American Anthropologist |date=12 October 1909 |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=563–594 |doi=10.1525/aa.1909.11.4.02a00030 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Bartlett">{{cite journal |last1=Bartlett |first1=John Russell |title=The Language of the Piro |journal=American Anthropologist |date=9 July 1909 |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=426–433 |doi=10.1525/aa.1909.11.3.02a00060 |url=https://doi.org/10.1525/aa.1909.11.3.02a00060 |access-date=3 July 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Piro-origin place names listed by Bandelier are Abo, Arti-puy, Genobey, Pataotry, Pil-abó, Qual-a-cú, Quelotetrey, Tabirá ([[Gran  Quivira]]), Ten-abó, Tey-pam-á, Trenaquel and Zen-ecú ([[Senecú]]).<ref name="Harrington"/>

==Vocabulary==
As Piro was morphologically [[agglutinative]], words were built from prefixes, stems and suffixes. For example, ''quen-lo-a-tu-ya-é'' ("mosquito") is [[Interlinear gloss|glossed]] as "the insect that bites".

Piro was reportedly [[mutually intelligible]] with [[Southern Tiwa language|Isleta]] with many shared words and case stems. Of the 180 words in Bartlett's Piro vocabulary, 87% were identical or nearly so to their corresponding stems in Southern Tiwa. The vocabulary created by Harrington also contains several  [[loanwords]] from Spanish, such as ''pipa-hem'' for "pipe" (from Spanish {{Lang|es|pipa}}).<ref name="Harrington"/>
